Why a log burner 1: zone your evenings

Why a log burner, reason 1: zone your evenings 🛋️

Most families live in one room after tea. A stove lets you turn the thermostat down and heat that room properly, instead of warming empty bedrooms.

We won’t invent a savings figure for you, because every house is different. That’s just the honest reason.

Chimney sweeping: book before winter

Lighting the fire this winter? Get the chimney swept first 🧹

Once a year for most people. If you burn wood hard all winter, twice is safer: once before the season and once part way through.

Guide prices:
• Chimney sweep & certificate: £65
• Sweep with smoke test: £85
• Bird’s nest removal: from £95

Sheets down, vacuum on, no mess left behind, and a certificate for your records. Bridgend, Porthcawl, Pyle and all round. Tell me the town and I’ll give you a day.

Questions Gareth gets every week (5-slide carousel)

The ones I get asked every week 👉 swipe

Do I need a working chimney?
No. With no chimney, Gareth runs a black twin-wall flue out through the wall and up the side of the house (£3,600–£3,800, cylinder stove included). In a single-storey extension the flue goes straight up through the roof (£2,300–£2,500). If your chimney stack has already been taken down, that’s a straight stove fit too (£1,375, stove extra). The free survey tells you which one you are. (All Gareth’s guide prices.)

Is the stove included?
On a full fireplace knockout, a twin-wall flue job and an extension, yes. On the two straight stove fits (£975 with the chimney stack in place, £1,375 with it removed) the stove is an extra cost. Gareth helps you choose one to suit the room and prices it with you on the survey. (Both Gareth’s guide prices, plus your stove.)

How long does it take?
A full fireplace knockout takes two to three days. Gareth tells you how long your job will take on the survey.

Are the prices on the site fixed?
They’re Gareth’s guide prices for a typical job. After the free survey you get one confirmed price in writing before anything starts, so you know exactly where you stand.

Not on here? Ask in the comments and I’ll answer it properly.

Why a log burner 2: modern stoves waste very little

Why a log burner, reason 2: modern stoves waste very little 🔥

A modern Ecodesign stove turns around three-quarters or more of the wood into heat in the room. An open fire manages nearer a fifth; the rest goes up the chimney.

And reason 3: a wood burner doesn’t care about power cuts or a boiler that’s given up. Dry logs in the store, warm house.

A knockout, day by day

Sheets down on day one. Fire lit at the end 🗓️

Day one, the mucky bit:
• 8am: dust sheets everywhere. Furniture moved, the room sealed off.
• Morning: the old fireplace is knocked out and the opening checked.
• Afternoon: cement boarded, and plastered where it’s needed.

Day two or three, the good bit:
• Morning: the slate hearth goes down and the stove is set in place.
• Afternoon: everything connected and checked, ready to be signed off with building regs.

A full fireplace knockout takes two to three days. I’ll tell you how long your job will take on the survey.

10Thu 15 Oct · 19:00Reel · 1.9 MB

Chimney repointing (film Reel)

When the mortar goes, the water comes in 🌧️

A stack sits in the worst of the weather. That damp patch on a bedroom ceiling usually started up on the chimney years earlier. Look out for:
• A damp patch on the chimney breast or the ceiling below
• Sand or bits of mortar in the gutter
• Grass or a weed growing out of the stack
• A pot sitting crooked, or cracked flaunching

Guide prices: chimney repointing from £450, and scaffolding, where a stack can’t be reached safely, from £350. Stack work is always looked at first, and you get the price before anything starts.

Best to get it sorted before the winter weather really sets in. Send me a photo of the stack on WhatsApp.

(The film and pictures show the kind of work Gareth does. They’re illustrations, not a customer’s home; his own job photos are on the way.)

First burn, done with you

I don’t just light it and leave 🔥

At the end of the job I light the first fire with you, show you the air controls and what to burn, and leave you with the building regs sign-off for your records.

New to stoves? Dry wood is the big one: kiln-dried or well-seasoned logs. Wet wood tars the glass and the flue and gives off a lot less heat.
